source.title: ReLATE: Learning Relative Representations for Post-Hoc Multimodal Alignment
source.authors: Shiwon Kim; JaeSeong Hong; Y. Park

record.file_problem: None; the full paper and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests post-hoc cross-modal representation alignment using learned relative representations and reports alignment-related consistency and downstream task results; this is a conceptual test rather than a reproduction of the original method.
record.gate_note: The study deliberately trains modality-specific anchors on paired image–text data, so its results are not evidence that independently trained models converge without alignment training or that alignment rises as model capability increases. The anchor-consistency analysis measures matched versus mismatched pairs at several top-k settings. The scaling analyses vary paired-data quantity, not model size or capability. Comparisons with other alignment methods are reported in the rows where they quantify ReLATE's outcomes; cited results from other work are not included.
record.test_reason: A methods paper. It builds cross-modal alignment on purpose by training anchors on paired image–caption data, with contrastive loss, between frozen DINOv2/UNI and text encoders. Every result compares ReLATE with other post-hoc alignment methods: task accuracy, retrieval, segmentation, grounding and pathology classification. The anchor-consistency Dice analysis measures a property of the trained alignment, not convergence that arises on its own. No result bears on whether independent models converge, with scale or otherwise. No result measures mapping loss against each encoder's own performance, so V4 is not tested either. Relative representations and the Platonic hypothesis are used only as motivation.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that ReLATE, training only modality-specific anchors with anchor-wise similarity pooling, outperforms the compared post-hoc alignment methods on all 13 general-domain benchmarks, across data scales and six encoder pairs. It also matches or exceeds the evaluated pathology VLMs on three zero-shot benchmarks. Stated limits: dependence on the semantic coverage of the paired data, and anchor roles that are not explicitly controlled.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a learned-anchor relative-representation alignment procedure with anchor-wise token pooling and paired contrastive training; it is not a reproduction of the original claim's measurement of convergence with model scale or capability.
record.method_sensitivity: Anchor consistency changes with top-k and with matched versus mismatched pairs. Reported task performance also varies by dataset and encoder pairing. Pooling temperature and number of anchors affect task averages, but those ablations test ReLATE design settings rather than convergence itself.

fits_no_version.finding: Training-free relative representations with fixed paired-sample anchors (ASIF) align DINOv2 and RoBERTa poorly. Retrieval averages 3.9% at K=512 and 17.1% at K=82K, against 59.2% for learned anchors (Table III, A2).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Off-the-shelf relative representations built from fixed paired anchors give weak cross-modal correspondence between separately pretrained vision and language encoders without learned alignment.

record.problems: The central alignment is induced by training anchors on paired data, so it does not establish spontaneous convergence. There is no model-size or capability sweep, and no separation of shared-data effects from other explanations. Anchor-consistency numeric values are largely figure-only; the analysis uses hard Dice rather than testing alternative metrics or OOD inputs. Several encoder-pair comparisons use a single seed. Downstream task scores do not directly quantify loss relative to each encoder's original task performance.
record.rows_left_out: No rows left out. Results varying paired-data quantity, anchor count, pooling temperature, pooling type, or encoder pair were not separately catalogued unless they measured the tested convergence/alignment versions; those results concern method design or task scaling rather than model-size/capability convergence.

untested.parts: No model-size or capability sweep; no convergence measure among independent models.
No measure of native vision–language alignment as encoders improve. Six encoder pairs are compared only on post-alignment task scores.
No comparison across seeds of shared features in independently trained networks.
No measure of mapping loss or interchangeability. Alignment is trained with paired contrastive loss and evaluated only against other alignment methods.
Anchor visualizations concern one trained alignment, not features recurring across models.
No test of how a convergence measure depends on metric, neighbours or inputs. The Dice and Jaccard analysis concerns trained anchors.
Nothing on plateau, incompleteness or causes of convergence.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T2' and its V4/V6 labels are overturned. All rows compare the study's own method with others, or measure overlap of anchors trained to align matched pairs. The study also selects layers by mutual-kNN similarity (block 23 / layer 24), but that is only a selection value. The fixed-anchor ASIF ablation is the closest to evidence on relative-representation interchangeability; it is recorded under fits_no_version.

versions.untested_parts: No sweep of model size or capability, and no measurement of convergence among independently trained models as they scale.
The paper aligns vision and language representations using paired data, but does not test whether alignment increases as both encoders improve in capability.
No comparison of same-architecture networks trained from different initializations for shared features or subspaces.
Tests paired-data, learned-anchor relative alignment and its task utility. Does not test unpaired mapping, stitching, linear-map loss, or preservation of each encoder's original task performance.
Anchor visualizations show semantic responses and reuse within learned models, not recurrence of the same interpretable features or circuits across different models.
Tests dependence on top-k and matched versus mismatched inputs using hard Dice. Does not compare alternative similarity metrics or test out-of-distribution inputs.
No experiment separates shared training data or objectives from a common model of reality as causes of alignment, nor tests whether alignment plateaus or remains incomplete.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Evaluated paired-data post-hoc alignment tasks, including general-domain and pathology benchmarks
reader_labels.reason: Learned relative representations support cross-modal task performance; ReLATE is best among compared post-hoc methods on the reported general-domain benchmarks and attains or exceeds reference VLM results on the three listed pathology datasets (r01–r18).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: DTD classification and ReferItGame grounding; SICAP pathology classification
reader_labels.reason: Reported gains are small on DTD and ReferItGame, and SICAP balanced accuracy is 38.3 ± 3.3 with all methods below 40%, showing task-dependent limitations rather than uniformly strong alignment (r04, r14, r17).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Matched versus mismatched image–caption pairs across the tested top-k settings on COCO and Flickr30k
reader_labels.reason: Matched pairs have greater anchor overlap than mismatched pairs at every tested k; the explicit top-1 values are 45.5% versus 0.9% on COCO and 27.9% versus 1.2% on Flickr30k, with mismatched scores described as near chance (r19–r38).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Increasing top-k from small to larger selections
reader_labels.reason: The matched–mismatched gap narrows as k grows, so the apparent consistency depends on the top-k setting; the study reports hard Dice only and does not establish dependence across alternative metrics or OOD inputs (r23–r38).
